---
title: "Julia Runtime Preparation"
subtitle: "How does the first backend operation obtain a reproducible Julia?"
toc-depth: 2
---

**Status:** `CONVERGING` implementation design.

## Prepare on the first backend-bound operation

The user installs SCNSim with `uv sync --locked`; no separate Julia setup step
is part of the Notebook UX. SCNSim ships static runtime metadata naming one
exact Julia patch version for that package release. The first operation that
needs Julia asks JuliaPkg for that version: JuliaPkg reuses an exact matching
system installation when available and otherwise installs it automatically.
See the official [JuliaPkg package documentation](https://pypi.org/project/juliapkg/).

JuliaPkg owns executable discovery and installation only. SCNSim does not use
JuliaPkg's managed project as its numerical environment. Every child process
uses the separate SCNSim-owned project described below.

Pure authoring and authoring-schematic operations do not prepare Julia.
`run.explain()` and the compiled schematic may prepare it because both need the
real compiler preflight. Preparation is dependency work, not a solver action
and not workspace evidence.

## Ship one internal Julia environment

SCNSim will commit these package resources:

```text
src/scnsim/_julia/
  Project.toml
  Manifest.toml
  runtime.json
  src/SCNSimBackend.jl
  bin/scnsim_request.jl
```

`runtime.json` binds Julia `1.12.6` and the versioned algorithm IDs. The first
slice Manifest contains JSON3, CMAEvolutionStrategy, and required standard
libraries only; JosephsonCircuits enters with HB. Python locates all resources
through `importlib.resources`, never caller cwd or a user Julia project.

SCNSim will commit one internal `Project.toml` and `Manifest.toml`. The package
launches the JuliaPkg-resolved executable with `--project` pointing to that
internal project and instantiates it when needed. A committed Manifest fixes
the resolved dependency state; Julia's environment guidance
documents that `instantiate` restores the packages recorded by a project and
Manifest ([Pkg environments](https://pkgdocs.julialang.org/v1.10/environments/)).

Semantic runtime identity records:

- SCNSim Python and Julia source-tree hashes;
- the exact Julia version;
- Project and Manifest hashes; and
- the versioned numerical algorithm identity.

A merely compatible version constraint is not enough to resolve an old
receipt.

Python computes this identity from package-owned static runtime metadata,
source manifests, and the committed Project/Manifest before launching Julia.
`resolve()` uses those same installed bytes and never selects, starts, or
queries an executable. The executable subsequently used for a new attempt must
report the declared exact Julia version or preparation fails before numerical
work.

The attempt separately records the actual executable hash, host OS and
architecture, CPU description, Julia threads, BLAS threads, and BLAS vendor.
Those execution resources do not rename the request. The Lessons 1--5
launcher fixes Julia and BLAS to one thread to reduce avoidable variation, but
still records the observed values. See
[Catalog and Runtime Identity](catalog-and-runtime-identity.qmd).

The first candidate supports Linux and macOS. Windows raises
`UnsupportedRuntimePlatformError` before workspace mutation, Julia selection,
or download.

## Fail without a hidden fallback

Offline mode uses only an already available exact-version Julia and cached
packages. If either is absent, preparation fails with the missing runtime or
package named. SCNSim does not silently switch environment, edit a user Julia
project, download during `resolve()`, or fall back to an unrecorded system
installation.

Precompilation belongs to environment preparation. Additional custom
precompile workloads are deferred until representative measurements show that
startup cost materially affects the one-process request boundary.
